where: the row status chips — "◷ Saving" and "◷ Waiting" — sitting in the same row as the "⚠ Allergy" chip
finding: The new sync chips are drawn with exactly the recipe the allergy flag already owns: same amber fill, same amber ring, same radius, same 11px semibold, same leading glyph slot. On Ava Chen's row two amber chips sit 90px apart meaning entirely unrelated things — one is a background job that is going fine, the other is a medical fact a leader must never miss. Amber on this screen used to mean one thing; it now means two, and the reader has to read every amber chip to find out which. Down 45 rows that is the difference between scanning and reading, which is the whole point of J2.
evidence: Row 1 (Ava Chen): "◷ Saving" and "⚠ Allergy" are pixel-identical badges apart from the glyph and the word. Row 6 (Priya Raman) shows "⚠ Allergy" alone in the same amber; row 2 (Marcus) shows "◷ Waiting" alone. Squinted at, rows 1, 2 and 6 all read as "something amber is wrong with this child".
direction: Amber has to keep meaning "a fact about the child" and the sync language has to be legible as a different class of object without a new hue. Separate them by form and weight rather than colour: let the standing flags keep the filled badge, and give the transient job states a quieter, obviously-temporary form — an outline-only or text-plus-glyph treatment, or a single glyph in its own fixed column with the word on hover — so that at a glance the amber blocks are facts and the sync marks are activity. Whatever is chosen, the allergy chip and a sync chip must never be the same shape in the same row.

where: the status strip's action buttons and the Edit profile / Remove from roster pair 16px beneath them
finding: The strip's actions use the page's primary button treatment, so the record now carries two brand-filled pills stacked sixteen pixels apart, and on sync-profile the loudest object above the fold is "Undo this edit" — an escape hatch for a job that is going perfectly well, on a screen whose entire message is "nothing is wrong, close the tab". The composition says act; the words say carry on. On sync-failed the same treatment produces two identical two-button pairs in the same order (blue, then ink) sixteen pixels apart, so "Fix and send again"/"Discard the edit" and "Edit profile"/"Remove from roster" are indistinguishable until read, and the one moment the design genuinely wants a loud primary has no way left to say so.
evidence: sync-profile: the blue "Undo this edit" pill inside the amber strip and the blue "Edit profile" pill below it are the same fill, radius, height and type. sync-failed: four buttons in two visually identical pairs, one above the other.
direction: Reserve the filled primary for the page's own action and let the strip speak at a lower weight by default — a quiet secondary or a text action for a healthy in-flight job, so the strip's message outranks its escape hatch. Let the strip earn the filled primary only in the states that require a human (failed, orphaned), and when it does, step the page's own primary down so there is one loudest thing on the record, not two.

where: the First name / Last name fields and the blue notice directly above them
finding: The two name fields render at disabled opacity with no reason anywhere in the frame, and the object immediately above them is a filled blue panel stating that Save writes name, grade, birthday and allergies to Planning Center. The modal contradicts itself in adjacent elements: a notice that promises Save writes these fields, sitting on top of fields that cannot be typed into. Worse, the fields still carry the neutral hint "Saved in Planning Center" — the same hint the editable Grade select carries — so the only signal that they are locked is a contrast drop, which on this ink ramp reads as "nothing here" rather than "held for a reason". Grade, the other field the record says is in flight, is fully bright and editable, so the dimming does not even read as a rule.
evidence: "Ava" and "Chen" sit at roughly half the contrast of "9th grade" and "03 / 14 / 2011" in the same form; the blue notice above them is the highest-contrast block in the modal.
direction: A locked field needs a reason attached to it, not just less contrast: the explanation of why the managed fields are held belongs inside the modal that actually renders, above or on the affected fields, and the standing blue notice needs to step out of the way while it is there — two filled panels stacked at the top of a 544px modal is one too many. And the hint under a held field must say something different from the hint under an editable one.

where: the whole frame — the modal and the record behind it
finding: sync-blocked is compositionally identical to sync-editor: same notice, same field order, same footer, the only difference being the four words of the title. Nothing in the frame distinguishes "this student's link is in flight and these fields are not yours yet" from an ordinary edit. The backdrop compounds it — the record dimmed behind "Edit Amara Whitfield" is Ava Chen's, name, grade, allergies and all, so the frame shows two different children at once and invites the reader to believe the form belongs to the record behind it.
evidence: Placing sync-editor--desktop-fold and sync-blocked--desktop-fold side by side, the only differing pixels are the title and the two name values; the dimmed header behind the modal reads "AC / Ava Chen / 9th grade / Allergies".
direction: The blocked state needs a visible object of its own in the modal that renders — the reason the managed fields are held, named at the top of the form — and the record behind a modal must be the record the modal is editing, so the backdrop is context rather than a contradiction.

where: the "Queued" chip on the Amara Whitfield row
finding: "Queued" is one of the state words the new language depends on, but it is drawn in the neutral ink chip used for "No contact" and "No birthday" and it sits at the far right of the flag cluster rather than in the fixed sync slot where "Saving", "Waiting" and "Needs you" appear. Two visual languages for one idea, in one table: a reader scanning the sync column down 45 rows will not see this row as having anything in flight, because it is neither in that column nor in that colour, and grouped where it is it reads as a data-completeness gap like the two chips beside it.
evidence: Amara Whitfield's row: "Visitor", "No contact", "Queued" packed right-aligned together, all the same neutral treatment; the sync slot after "7th grade" on that row is empty, while every other in-flight row has its chip there.
direction: One slot and one treatment for anything that is in flight with Planning Center, whatever the flavour of the job — a pending link belongs in the sync column with the pending edits. If a pending link deserves less urgency than a pending edit, say that with weight inside the sync language, not by moving it into the flags.

where: the dotted pending underline under "Chen-Ito" and "10th grade" in the record header
finding: On the grade line the annotation is brighter than the thing it annotates: an amber dotted rule under 14px ink-500 text, so the eye lands on the mark and not on the value. A mark that says "this is what she is now called" should not out-contrast the name it is marking. It also has to share the page with two solid underlines that mean links ("Open their profile", "Change it there"), so the header carries three underline treatments with two unrelated meanings.
evidence: In the header crop the dotted amber rule under "10th grade" is the highest-contrast element of that line; the h1's dotted rule sits close enough to the baseline of bold 20px text to read as a spellcheck squiggle.
direction: Keep the pending value at full reading contrast and damp the mark — the underline should be the quieter of the two, not the louder. Consider lifting a pending value to the normal ink level while it is pending so the mark is the only thing that differs, and give the dotted rule more offset from a bold heading so it reads as annotation rather than as an error squiggle.

where: the empty middle column of each row, between the name and the "Sat" column
finding: Every row reserves roughly 350px between the truncated name and the last-seen date and puts nothing in it, while "Marcus Delacroix-Oy…" truncates mid-word 350px short of the space that would have held it. Meanwhile the new sync chip has been dropped into the right-hand cluster, which on Ava's row is now four objects deep. The table has an empty third in the middle and a crowded third at the end, which reads as a layout that grew rather than one that was set — the opposite of the well-set table density is meant to look like.
evidence: Rows 1 and 2 show the name truncating at a fixed 192px while the band from x≈700 to x≈1000 is blank in all 45 rows; Ava's row carries grade, sync chip and allergy chip crammed into the last 320px.
direction: Spend the dead middle. Either let the name column breathe so surnames stop truncating, or move the sync mark out of the flag cluster and into that empty band, next to the name it belongs to — which also puts distance between the sync mark and the amber allergy chip and solves half of the amber problem for free.

where: the status strip's shape and position at 1440px
finding: The strip shares the cards' radius, ring and 16px rhythm, which is right — but it is a full-column band, 133px tall, placed above everything, so a fourteen-second background job is physically the largest object on a child's record and pushes the facts a leader came for further down a column that is already only 640px wide in a 1440px window. Half the window is empty to the right of it. A pointer-width record has somewhere to put a transient status that a phone does not.
evidence: Above the fold on sync-profile the strip occupies more vertical space than the identity block and the button row combined, and the area from x≈1152 to x≈1440 is empty for the full height of the page.
direction: At pointer widths let the strip take a shape that suits a wide window — a single-line strip with its action inline, or an aside set beside the identity block rather than stacked above the record — so that in-flight status is present and legible without being the biggest object on a child's page. The stacked band stays right on the phone.
